extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy (ethics), instructors and scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Aristotle's account of the Chief Good (Happiness/eudaimonia): criteria for what counts as the final human good, the nature of virtue (intellectual and moral), how virtues are acquired, and the role of external goods and life-duration in constituting a flourishing life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chief Good must be final
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chief Good is 'that for the sake of which the other things are done' — i.e., an end chosen for its own sake rather than as a means to something else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish final ends from instrumental ends (wealth, tools, etc.). If multiple ends exist, the most final (never chosen as a means) is the Chief Good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chief Good must be self-sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: The final good should be 'self-sufficient' — taken alone makes life choice-worthy and leaves one wanting for nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-sufficiency is not only for a solitary individual but for the person's household, friends, and political community (up to a reasonable limit). Do not extend indefinitely (friends' friends etc.). Consider social embeddedness when judging sufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness is chosen for its own sake
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness (eudaimonia) is something we choose always for its own sake and never with a view to something further; other goods (honour, pleasure, intellect) are chosen both for themselves and as means to happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as a litmus: if an alleged good is ever chosen primarily as a means, it is not the Chief Good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness is activity of the soul in accordance with excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Good of man is 'a working of the soul in the way of Excellence' — i.e., activity consonant with the best and most perfect Excellence/virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogize to crafts: the excellence of a harpist is playing the harp well; human excellence is rational activity performed excellently. Emphasize activity (performance) over mere possession of traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness requires a complete life (duration criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness (blessedness) is not a transient state; it requires 'in a complete life' (ἐν βίῳ τελείῳ) — many days or a full span, not a single event or short period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess flourishing over whole-life patterns rather than momentary experiences. One day or brief success does not establish happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: possession vs use (state vs activity)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a difference between having virtue (a state/habit) and exercising it (activity). The state/habit can exist without producing good (e.g., a sleeping virtuous person), whereas activity necessarily does good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer evaluative judgments based on exercised virtues (actions) rather than mere possession of dispositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtuous actions are pleasant to the truly virtuous
rubrics_metrics.description: A truly good person takes pleasure in noble actions; the perfected state involves taking pleasure in acting virtuously, not merely acting under compulsion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the agent's affective responses as a test: if someone abstains from wrongdoing but feels pain or regret, they lack perfected self-mastery; if they do right with pleasure, they are virtuous.

rubrics_metrics.name: External goods are necessary but not primary
rubrics_metrics.description: External goods (friends, wealth, political influence, good birth, offspring, beauty) are instrumental 'in a manner' and their possession helps enable noble actions; extreme lack can mar blessedness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize external goods as facilitating instruments; complete deprivation (very ugly, ill-born, solitary, bad children) can prevent flourishing. Balance internal virtue criteria with pragmatic needs for external support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness requires complete virtue and co-operative goods
rubrics_metrics.description: To constitute Happiness there must be 'complete virtue and a complete life,' and certain co-operative external goods are needed as instruments for acting nobly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate candidates for happiness by checking for (a) pervasive virtuous activity across life and (b) sufficient external conditions to exercise virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness is more like 'blessed' than simply 'praised'
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness belongs to the class of things 'precious and final' (blessed), not merely praiseworthy like individual virtues that are praised for making men apt to do noble acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When ranking goods, treat happiness as the ultimate standard to which praise-bearing virtues are referential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human function: rational activity
rubrics_metrics.description: The work (function) of Man is 'a working of the soul in accordance with reason' — the proper function distinguishes human good from plant/animal life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify human excellence by evaluating activities that uniquely manifest reason (contemplation, practical reasoning, moral action).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual vs Moral virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Human Excellence divides into Intellectual (science, intelligence, practical wisdom) and Moral (liberality, perfected self-mastery). The Intellectual typically arises from teaching and time, the Moral from habituation and custom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess intellectual virtues by education and deliberative capacities; assess moral virtues by habituated patterns of action and social upbringing/laws. Different pedagogical approaches are appropriate for each.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral virtues arise by habituation (practice) not by nature alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral virtues are formed neither simply by nature nor in spite of it; nature gives capacity, but virtues are perfected through repeated actions (doing just acts makes one just, doing brave acts makes one brave).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate moral excellence by history of actions/habits. Legal and educational institutions should cultivate right habits (lawgivers aim to make members good by habituation). Anti-pattern: expecting virtues to appear without training and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue is a mean between excess and defect
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral qualities are spoiled by deficiency and excess; the virtuous state is the 'mean' preserving the right measure (e.g., cowardice—bravery—rashness; overindulgence—self-mastery—insensibility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge actions and dispositions by their proportionality; identify excess/defect and aim for the intermediate. Use analogies in health/strength and temperance to determine proper measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing formation of habits via pleasure/pain responses
rubrics_metrics.description: A test of habituation: the perfected person experiences pleasure or at least absence of pain in right actions (e.g., self-master who abstains and is glad; brave who faces danger with pleasure or without pain).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess moral development by observing emotional responses post-action: genuine pleasure indicates internalized virtue; persistent distress suggests merely outward conformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical reasoning (Right Reason) as guiding standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Acting 'in accordance with Right Reason' is the general maxim for moral action; particulars require judgement and cannot be captured by exact rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use practical wisdom (phronesis) to apply general principles to particular cases; accept that moral deliberation admits of approximation, context-sensitivity, and expert judgment rather than rigid rule-following.
